---
id: document-group
title: DocumentGroup
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/documentgroup.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/file-management.md
---

# DocumentGroup

The scene for document-based apps, with New, Open, and Save built in.

Also called: document-based app, document app, documents, NSDocument, NSDocumentController, FileDocument, ReferenceFileDocument, open panel, save panel, NSOpenPanel.

## Contents

- Use when
- Built from
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- `DocumentGroup` makes your app document-based.
- You give it a document type and the view that edits it.
- SwiftUI adds File > New and the standard document commands, shows the system's open and save panels, opens each document in its own window, and writes the file back when people save.
- Model the document as a struct that conforms to `FileDocument`, and SwiftUI registers undo for every change.
- If it has to be a class, use `ReferenceFileDocument` and register undo yourself.

## Built from

DocumentGroup(newDocument:)
└── editor view
    └── file.$document

## Rules

- **Start new documents as “Untitled”.** That's the name the system gives a new document until people pick one in the save panel. Keep it, rather than inventing your own.
- **Save people's work without asking.** Save periodically while people edit, and when they close the document or switch apps, so work isn't lost.
- **Use the system's open and save panels.** People know them from every other Mac app. Build your own file browser only for a strong reason.
- **Hide file extensions by default.** Let people show them if they want, and respect that choice in every open and save panel.

## Pitfalls

- **Every document-based app declares its types.** List the content types your app opens under Document Types (`CFBundleDocumentTypes`) in the target's Info pane.
- **With several document groups, order matters.** SwiftUI opens a file with the first group whose types match it, so put more specific types first.

**Note:** Apple's documentation marks `FileDocument` deprecated in macOS 27.2, in favor of the new `Document` protocol, which needs macOS 27. For an app that also runs on earlier versions, `FileDocument` is still the one to use.

## Key APIs

- `DocumentGroup(newDocument:editor:)`: Creates, opens, and edits one document type.
- `FileDocument`: A struct document. Undo comes for free.
- `ReferenceFileDocument`: A class document. You register undo.
- `readableContentTypes`: The file types the document opens.
- `init(configuration:)`: Reads the document from a file.
- `fileWrapper(configuration:)`: Writes the document to a file.
- `file.$document`: A binding that edits the open document.
- `file.fileURL`: Where it's saved; `nil` until the first save.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@main
struct EditorApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        DocumentGroup(newDocument: TextFile()) { file in
            TextEditor(text: file.$document.text)
        }
    }
}
```

### A plain-text document

A `FileDocument` lists the types it reads, loads itself in `init(configuration:)`, and writes itself in `fileWrapper(configuration:)`.

```swift
import SwiftUI
import UniformTypeIdentifiers

struct TextFile: FileDocument {
    static let readableContentTypes = [UTType.plainText]
    var text = ""

    init() {}

    init(configuration: ReadConfiguration) throws {
        guard let data = configuration.file.regularFileContents else {
            throw CocoaError(.fileReadCorruptFile)
        }
        text = String(decoding: data, as: UTF8.self)
    }

    func fileWrapper(configuration: WriteConfiguration) throws -> FileWrapper {
        FileWrapper(regularFileWithContents: Data(text.utf8))
    }
}
```

**Important:** SwiftUI reads and writes documents on a background thread. Don't update the interface from those two methods.

### Show where the file is saved

The editor closure also gets `fileURL`, which is `nil` until the first save. Use it for display, and let the document read and write the file.

```swift
DocumentGroup(newDocument: TextFile()) { file in
    TextEditor(text: file.$document.text)
        .safeAreaInset(edge: .bottom) {
            Text(file.fileURL?.lastPathComponent ?? "Not saved yet")
                .font(.caption)
                .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
                .padding(6)
        }
}
```

### Your own file type

```swift
extension UTType {
    static let checklist = UTType(exportedAs: "com.example.checklist")
}

struct ChecklistFile: FileDocument {
    static let readableContentTypes = [UTType.checklist]
    var items: [String] = []

    init() {}

    init(configuration: ReadConfiguration) throws {
        let data = configuration.file.regularFileContents ?? Data()
        items = try JSONDecoder().decode([String].self, from: data)
    }

    func fileWrapper(configuration: WriteConfiguration) throws -> FileWrapper {
        FileWrapper(regularFileWithContents: try JSONEncoder().encode(items))
    }
}
```

## Related

`file-import-export`, `document-editor`, `undo-redo`, `app-sandbox`, `window-group`

---
id: window-style
title: Window style & sizing
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/windows.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/windows.md
---

# Window style & sizing

Scene modifiers for a window's title bar, toolbar style, size, and position.

Also called: windowStyle, hiddenTitleBar, title bar, titlebar, transparent title bar, windowToolbarStyle, unified toolbar, expanded toolbar, defaultSize, window size.

## Contents

- Use when
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- These modifiers go on a scene in your `App`, like a `WindowGroup`, not on a view.
- They decide how new windows start out.
- People can still move and resize them, within the limits you set.
- A few window behaviors are view modifiers instead, like `.containerBackground(_:for:)` with `.window`, so you can set them from inside the window.

## Rules

- **Keep the system's window frame.** People know how standard windows look and behave. A homemade frame or window buttons that don't match exactly make the app feel broken.
- **Let windows adapt to any size.** People arrange windows side by side and resize them all the time. Set a minimum that keeps your layout intact, and let it grow from there.
- **Keep important things out of a bottom bar.** People often move a window so its bottom edge is off screen. Use a bottom bar only for a little status, like Finder's item count.
- **Keep the system's look for each window state.** People tell the active window apart by its colored window buttons and materials. Standard backgrounds and controls change with the state; custom ones have to do it themselves.

## Pitfalls

- **Settings windows fit their content by default.** With `.automatic` resizability, a `Settings` window uses `.contentSize` and every other scene uses `.contentMinSize`.
- **These are starting values.** When the system restores a window, it comes back at the size and place people left it.

## Key APIs

`.defaultSize(width:height:)`, `.windowResizability(.contentSize)`, `.defaultPosition(.topTrailing)`, `.windowStyle(.hiddenTitleBar)`, `.windowToolbarStyle(.unified)`, `.containerBackground(_:for:)`, `WindowDragGesture()`, `.windowResizeBehavior(.disabled)`

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@main
struct LibraryApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
                .frame(minWidth: 480, minHeight: 320)
        }
        .defaultSize(width: 900, height: 600)
    }
}
```

### A minimum size and a starting size

A `frame(minWidth:minHeight:)` on the content sets how small the window can get. `.defaultSize` sets the size it opens at.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    ContentView()
        .frame(minWidth: 320, minHeight: 180)
}
.defaultSize(width: 440, height: 260)
```

**Note:** A default size outside what the window allows is clamped to fit.

### A window that fits its content

`.windowResizability(.contentSize)` takes the window's limits from the content's frame. A fixed frame makes a window people can't resize.

```swift
Window("About Notes", id: "about") {
    AboutView()
        .frame(width: 440, height: 560)
}
.windowResizability(.contentSize)
.defaultPosition(.center)
```

**Note:** To turn off resizing, minimizing, or full screen from inside a window, set `.windowResizeBehavior`, `.windowMinimizeBehavior`, and `.windowFullScreenBehavior` to `.disabled`, as the Timer window does.

### Where the window opens

The first window opens in the center of the screen. `.defaultPosition` picks another spot, given as a `UnitPoint`.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    ContentView()
}
.defaultPosition(.topTrailing)
```

### Toolbar styles

`.windowToolbarStyle` sets how the title and toolbar share the top of the window. Pick a style to compare.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    ContentView()
}
.windowToolbarStyle(.unifiedCompact)
```

### Hide the title bar

`.windowStyle(.hiddenTitleBar)` hides the title and the title bar's backing, so more of the content shows.

```swift
WindowGroup {
    PlayerView()
}
.windowStyle(.hiddenTitleBar)
.windowBackgroundDragBehavior(.enabled)
```

**Important:** Without a title bar, people need another place to grab the window. Set `.windowBackgroundDragBehavior` to `.enabled` so they can drag it by its background.

### A see-through window

From inside the window, `.containerBackground(_:for:)` with `.window` sets its background, and you can hide the toolbar's title and backing.

```swift
struct NowPlayingView: View {
    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            Text("Now Playing")
                .font(.title)
        }
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
        .containerBackground(.thinMaterial, for: .window)
        .toolbarBackgroundVisibility(.hidden, for: .windowToolbar)
        .toolbar(removing: .title)
        .gesture(WindowDragGesture())
        .allowsWindowActivationEvents()
    }
}
```

**Note:** `WindowDragGesture` lets people move the window by dragging the view. `.allowsWindowActivationEvents()` lets the drag work even while the window is in the background.

## Related

`window-group`, `window`, `toolbar`, `materials`, `full-screen`, `windows-layout`

# Opening windows

`opening-windows` · macOS · macOS 13.0+
Docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/openwindowaction.md · HIG: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/windows.md

Open, bring forward, and close windows from your own code.

## Use when

- Read `openWindow` from the environment and call it with a scene's ID, a value, or both.
- A `Window` comes to the front.
- A `WindowGroup` opens a new window, unless one is already showing that value.
- To close a window, call `dismiss` from a view inside it, or `dismissWindow` with the scene's ID from anywhere in your app.

## Rules

- **Pick the moments that deserve a window.** A new window helps people compare or keep context, like a draft next to the inbox. Opening one for everything clutters the screen.
- **Make “Open in New Window” easy to find.** Offer it in the item's context menu or the File menu, so it's there for people who want it.

## Pitfalls

- **Opening the same value twice doesn't make two windows.** If a window already shows that value, SwiftUI brings it to the front.
- **`pushWindow` is visionOS only.** It swaps one window for another there. On the Mac, open the new window and dismiss the old one.

## Guide

Read `openWindow` from the environment and call it with a scene's ID, a value, or both. A `Window` comes to the front. A `WindowGroup` opens a new window, unless one is already showing that value.

To close a window, call `dismiss` from a view inside it, or `dismissWindow` with the scene's ID from anywhere in your app.

### Usage

```swift
struct ShowActivityButton: View {
    @Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow

    var body: some View {
        Button("Show Activity") {
            openWindow(id: "activity")
        }
    }
}
```

### Two groups, one type

If two window groups take the same type, like a `UUID` for both messages and accounts, give each an `id` and pass both to `openWindow`.

```swift
WindowGroup("Message", id: "message", for: UUID.self) { $id in
    MessageView(id: id)
}
WindowGroup("Account", id: "account", for: UUID.self) { $id in
    AccountView(id: id)
}

// Elsewhere:
openWindow(id: "account", value: account.id)
```

## Key APIs

- `@Environment(\.openWindow)`: The action that opens windows.
- `openWindow(id:)`: Opens a scene by its ID.
- `openWindow(value:)`: Opens the window group for that value's type.

## Related

`window-group`, `window`, `commands`, `context-menu`, `keyboard-shortcuts`

# Search

`search` · macOS · macOS 12.0+
Docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/adding-a-search-interface-to-your-app.md · HIG: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/search-fields.md

A search field in the toolbar or sidebar, with suggestions and tokens.

## Use when

- Add `.searchable(text:)` to a `NavigationSplitView` or `NavigationStack`, or a view inside one, and a search field appears at the trailing edge of the window's toolbar.
- You own the text, and filter your data with it; SwiftUI draws and manages the field.
- With `placement: .sidebar`, the field sits at the top of the sidebar instead, which suits search that filters the sidebar itself.

## Rules

- **Say what people can search for.** Placeholder text like “Songs, Artists, Albums” tells people what the field covers before they type.
- **Put search at the trailing end of the toolbar.** It's the familiar spot in apps like Mail and Notes, and people can browse results while their selection stays visible in the detail.
- **Use the top of the sidebar for filtering the sidebar.** When search narrows down the sidebar's own items, like System Settings, a field at its top makes the link clear.
- **Suggest searches, and pair tokens with suggestions.** Recent or likely searches help people search faster, and suggestions teach which tokens exist.

## Pitfalls

- **Search as people type.** Filtering on every keystroke feels responsive. For slow searches, like ones over the network, wait for Return with `.onSubmit(of: .search)`.
- **This app does it.** Its sidebar search uses `placement: .sidebar`, and Go > Search (⌘F) focuses the field with `searchFocused`.

## Built from

NavigationSplitView
├── sidebar
├── detail
└── .searchable(text:)
    └── .searchSuggestions { }

`.searchable(text:prompt:)`, `placement: .sidebar`, `.searchSuggestions { }`, `.searchCompletion(_:)`, `.searchable(text:tokens:)`, `.searchFocused(_:)`, `.onSubmit(of: .search)`

# Commands & menu bar

`commands` · macOS · macOS 11.0+
Docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/building-and-customizing-the-menu-bar-with-swiftui.md · HIG: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/the-menu-bar.md

Add your own menus and menu items to the Mac's menu bar.

## Use when

- `.commands` adds menus and items to the menu bar from your `App`.
- `CommandMenu` makes a new menu, which the system puts between View and Window.
- `CommandGroup` adds items to a menu the system already has, or replaces some of them.
- Commands aren't inside any window, so they read `@FocusedValue` to find out what's in front and act on it.

## Rules

- **Dim commands that don't apply. Don't hide them.** A menu that keeps the same items teaches people what the app can do, even when a command isn't available right now.
- **End a command with an ellipsis when it asks for more.** The … tells people a window or dialog opens next, so choosing the item doesn't act right away.
- **Put every command in the menu bar.** People look there first when they're learning an app. A command in the menu bar can have a shortcut and works with Full Keyboard Access, even if it's also in a toolbar or context menu.
- **Keep menu titles short, and in the usual order.** One word fits best. Custom menus sit between View and Window, from the most general to the most specific.

## Pitfalls

- **Scenes bring the standard menus.** A `WindowGroup` already has Copy, Paste, and the window commands, and a `Settings` scene adds Settings… to the app menu. Add only what's yours.
- **Values in `FocusedValues` are always optional.** A value is `nil` while no focused window or view publishes it, which is your cue to disable the command.

**Note:** `CommandGroup(replacing:)` removes the system's items in that group. Replacing `.newItem` removes File > New.

## Built from

WindowGroup
└── .commands
    ├── CommandMenu("Story")
    │   ├── Button
    │   ├── Divider
    │   └── Toggle
    └── CommandGroup(after: .newItem)
        └── Button

## Key APIs

`.commands { }`, `CommandMenu(_:)`, `CommandGroup(after:)`, `CommandGroup(replacing:)`, `@FocusedValue`, `.focusedSceneValue(_:_:)`, `.focusedValue(_:_:)`, `SidebarCommands()`

---
id: keyboard-shortcuts
title: Keyboard shortcuts
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/keyboardshortcut(_:modifiers:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/keyboards.md
---

# Keyboard shortcuts

Run a button or menu item from the keyboard, like ⌘S for Save.

Also called: hotkey, hot key, key equivalent, keyEquivalent, accelerator, keybinding, key binding, command key, KeyEquivalent, EventModifiers.

## Default code

```swift
Button("Mark as Read") {
    markAsRead()
}
.keyboardShortcut("k", modifiers: [.command, .shift])
```

**Important:** A capital letter adds Shift: `.keyboardShortcut("K")` is ⇧⌘K. Write the letter in lowercase and list the modifiers, so the code says what people press.

## Rules

- **Don't give a standard shortcut a new job.** People expect ⌘C, ⌘Z, ⌘W, and the rest to work the same in every app. Pick a new shortcut for your own command instead.
- **Add shortcuts only for the commands people use most.** A few well-chosen shortcuts speed people up. Too many new ones make the app feel hard to learn.
- **Lead with Command, and add Shift for a related command.** Use Option sparingly, for advanced commands. Avoid Control: the system uses it for moving focus, screenshots, and more.
- **Write modifiers in the order ⌃ ⌥ ⇧ ⌘.** Menus list them that way, so help text and tooltips should too.
- **Don't add a modifier to make an unrelated shortcut.** ⇧⌘Z means Redo because ⌘Z means Undo. Using it for something else breaks the pattern people rely on.

## Pitfalls

- **A shortcut works anywhere in the front window.** Pressing it is the same as clicking the control, even when the control doesn't have focus.
- **The first match wins.** SwiftUI looks in the key window, then the main window, then the menu bar, and runs the first control it finds with that shortcut.
- **Shortcuts adapt to other keyboards.** The system remaps ones that are hard to type on another layout, like ⌘[, and mirrors directional ones for right-to-left languages.

## Key APIs

- `.keyboardShortcut(_:modifiers:)`: A key plus modifiers; ⌘ by default.
- `.keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)`: Return, for the main button.
- `.keyboardShortcut(.cancelAction)`: Escape, for Cancel.
- `KeyEquivalent`: The key: a character, or `.return`, `.delete`, arrows.
- `EventModifiers`: `.command`, `.shift`, `.option`, `.control`.

## Variants

### Return and Escape in a dialog

`.defaultAction` binds Return to the main button and `.cancelAction` binds Escape to Cancel, like a dialog.

```swift
HStack {
    Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) { dismiss() }
        .keyboardShortcut(.cancelAction)
    Button("Save") { save() }
        .keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)
}
```

### Shortcuts appear in menus

Add `.keyboardShortcut` to a button in a `Menu` or a `CommandMenu`, and the menu shows the keys beside it.

```swift
Menu("Message") {
    Button("Reply") { reply() }
        .keyboardShortcut("r")
    Button("Forward") { forward() }
        .keyboardShortcut("f", modifiers: [.command, .shift])
    Button("Mark as Unread") { markAsUnread() }
        .keyboardShortcut("u", modifiers: [.command, .shift])
}
```

**Note:** The shortcuts work while the button's window is in front, even with the menu closed. In a real app, put these in a `CommandMenu` so they work from the menu bar.

## Related

`commands`, `button`, `keyboard-access`, `focus-keyboard`

---
id: tooltips
title: Tooltips
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/help(_:)-6oiyb.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/offering-help.md
---

# Tooltips

A short phrase that appears when the pointer rests on a control.

Also called: help tag, toolTip, title attribute, hover text, help(_:), NSView toolTip, hint, icon button.

## Default code

```swift
Button("Restore Defaults", systemImage: "arrow.counterclockwise") {
    restoreDefaults()
}
.labelStyle(.iconOnly)
.help("Restore default settings")
```

**Important:** An icon on its own rarely says what a button does. Give every icon-only button a title for VoiceOver and a `.help` tooltip for everyone else.

## Rules

- **Say what the control does, in a few words.** Start with a verb, and keep it to 60 to 75 characters at most. A sentence fragment without articles is fine.
- **Don't repeat the control's name.** The name is already on screen or in the label. Use the space to explain what happens.
- **Describe only that control.** People hold the pointer over one control to learn about it, not about its neighbors or the whole task.
- **Use sentence case, and match the state.** Write “Pin note”, not “Pin Note”, and skip the final period. If the control changes, like Pin and Unpin, change the tooltip too.

## Pitfalls

- **`.help` is also the VoiceOver hint.** One modifier gives pointer users a tooltip and VoiceOver users a hint.
- **Tooltips wait for the pointer.** They appear only after the pointer rests on a control for a moment, so keep anything people must know in the window itself.

## Key APIs

- `.help(_:)`: Adds a tooltip and an accessibility hint.
- `.help(Text)`: The same, from a `Text`.
- `Button(_:systemImage:action:)`: A button with a title and a symbol.
- `.labelStyle(.iconOnly)`: Shows only a label's icon; the title stays for VoiceOver.

## Variants

### Icon-only toolbar buttons

Add `.help` to each icon-only toolbar button, so people can find out what it does before they click.

```swift
.toolbar {
    Button("New Note", systemImage: "square.and.pencil") { newNote() }
        .help("Create a note")
    Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up") { share() }
        .help("Send this note to someone")
    Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash") { delete() }
        .help("Move this note to the Trash")
}
```

**Note:** Hold the pointer over each symbol in the preview. A real `.toolbar` here would land in this window's own toolbar, so the preview draws one.

### A tooltip that follows the state

When a button switches between two actions, switch its `.help` text too, so it describes the next click.

```swift
@State private var isPinned = false

Button(isPinned ? "Unpin" : "Pin", systemImage: isPinned ? "pin.slash" : "pin") {
    isPinned.toggle()
}
.labelStyle(.iconOnly)
.help(isPinned ? "Unpin this note" : "Pin this note to the top")
```

## Related

`button`, `hover`, `toolbar`, `voiceover`

id: hover
title: Hover & pointer
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/onhover(perform:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pointing-devices.md
---

# Hover & pointer

React when the pointer moves over a view, and show the right pointer.

Also called: :hover, mouseenter, mouseleave, mousemove, cursor, NSCursor, NSTrackingArea, onHover, onContinuousHover, pointerStyle.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var isHovering = false

ProjectRow(project)
    .padding(8)
    .background(isHovering ? Color.secondary.opacity(0.15) : .clear,
                in: .rect(cornerRadius: 8))
    .onHover { isHovering = $0 }
```

**Note:** `.onHover` is like CSS `:hover`, except you store the state yourself and style the view from it.

## Rules

- **Show the pointer that matches what happens.** Each pointer has a meaning people know: a pointing hand for a link, an open hand for content they can pan, like a map, and a crosshair for precise selection. Don't use one for anything else.
- **Let the pointer bring back controls that fade away.** Controls that hide to keep the view calm, like playback controls over a video, should reappear when the pointer moves over them.
- **Keep every way of working consistent.** People switch between the pointer, the keyboard, and gestures without thinking. An action shouldn't work differently, or only work, with one of them.

## Pitfalls

- **The hover area is the view's frame.** Add padding before `.onHover` to make the area bigger.
- **`.pointerStyle` needs macOS 15.** `.onContinuousHover` needs macOS 14, and `.onHover` dates back to macOS 10.15.

## Key APIs

- `.onHover { isHovering in }`: Runs when the pointer enters or leaves.
- `.onContinuousHover { phase in }`: Reports the pointer's location as it moves.
- `.pointerStyle(_:)`: The pointer to show over a view.
- `.link`, `.grabIdle`, `.columnResize`: A few of the built-in pointer styles.
- `.pointerVisibility(.hidden)`: Hides the pointer over a view.

## Variants

### Show actions on the row under the pointer

Use `.onHover` to track the row under the pointer and show its buttons only there, so the list stays calm.

```swift
@State private var hoveredRow: Project.ID?

ForEach(projects) { project in
    HStack {
        Text(project.name)
        Spacer()
        if hoveredRow == project.id {
            Button("Share", systemImage: "square.and.arrow.up") { share(project) }
            Button("Delete", systemImage: "trash") { delete(project) }
        }
    }
    .labelStyle(.iconOnly)
    .buttonStyle(.borderless)
    .contentShape(.rect)
    .onHover { isHovering in
        hoveredRow = isHovering ? project.id : nil
    }
}
```

**Important:** Hover-only buttons are invisible to the keyboard and to VoiceOver until the pointer arrives. Put the same commands in a context menu or the menu bar.

### Follow the pointer

`.onContinuousHover` reports the pointer's location while it moves over a view, and `.ended` when it leaves.

```swift
@State private var spot: CGPoint?

SceneryView(.lake)
    .overlay {
        if let spot {
            Circle()
                .fill(.white.opacity(0.35))
                .frame(width: 60, height: 60)
                .position(spot)
        }
    }
    .onContinuousHover { phase in
        switch phase {
        case .active(let location): spot = location
        case .ended: spot = nil
        }
    }
```

### A resize pointer on a divider

`.pointerStyle(.columnResize)` shows the left-right resize pointer, so people know they can drag the divider.

```swift
@State private var sidebarWidth = 140.0

HStack(spacing: 0) {
    Sidebar()
        .frame(width: sidebarWidth)
    Rectangle()
        .fill(.separator)
        .frame(width: 1)
        .padding(.horizontal, 3)
        .contentShape(.rect)
        .pointerStyle(.columnResize)
        .gesture(DragGesture(coordinateSpace: .named("split")).onChanged { drag in
            sidebarWidth = min(max(drag.location.x, 100), 220)
        })
    Detail()
}
.coordinateSpace(.named("split"))
```

**Note:** For a real sidebar, `NavigationSplitView` gives you the divider and the pointer for free.

## Related

`tooltips`, `trackpad-gestures`, `drag-drop`, `button`

---
id: drag-drop
title: Drag and drop
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 26.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/drag-and-drop.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/drag-and-drop.md
---

# Drag and drop

Let people drag content within a window, between windows, and to other apps.

## Use when

- `.draggable` turns a view into something people can drag, and `.dropDestination` makes a view accept drops.
- Both work with `Transferable` types, so the same code handles drags inside a window, between your app's windows, and to and from other apps.
- A type's transfer representations decide what it becomes: your own data when it lands in your app, and plain text or a file in apps that don't know your type.

## Rules

- **Support drag and drop wherever people might try it.** Most people know it and try it everywhere. Text fields and text views already support it.
- **Offer another way to do the same thing.** Some people can't or don't drag. Back every drag with menu commands, like Copy and Paste or Move To.
- **Show whether a destination accepts the drop.** Highlight a destination only while content is over it and only if it can take it. Remove the highlight as soon as the pointer leaves.
- **Move within a container, copy between containers.** Dropping in the same place, like reordering a list, moves the content. Dropping somewhere else copies it, and a drop into another app always copies.
- **Let people drag content to the Finder.** Give it a file format your app can open again, the way Calendar drags an event out as an .ics file.
- **Offer the richest version first.** List your type's representations from highest fidelity to lowest, so each destination takes the best one it understands.

## Pitfalls

- **Common types already work.** `String`, `URL`, and many other system types conform to `Transferable`, so you can drag them without extra code.
- **A drag offers a copy unless you allow a move.** Pass `DragConfiguration(allowMove: true)` to `.dragConfiguration(_:)`. People can then hold ⌘ to move, or ⌥ to copy.
- **This `.dropDestination` is new in macOS 26.** It replaces the version with an `isTargeted:` closure, which is deprecated.

## Guide

`.draggable` turns a view into something people can drag, and `.dropDestination` makes a view accept drops. Both work with `Transferable` types, so the same code handles drags inside a window, between your app's windows, and to and from other apps.

A type's transfer representations decide what it becomes: your own data when it lands in your app, and plain text or a file in apps that don't know your type.

### Usage

```swift
@State private var basket: [String] = []

Text("Sunflowers")
    .draggable("Sunflowers")

BasketView(items: basket)
    .dropDestination(for: String.self) { names, session in
        basket.append(contentsOf: names)
    }
```

## Key APIs

`.draggable(_:)`, `.draggable(_:preview:)`, `.dropDestination(for:)`, `.onDropSessionUpdated(_:)`, `Transferable`, `CodableRepresentation`, `ProxyRepresentation`, `.dragConfiguration(_:)`

## Variants

### Drag text onto a target

Make each chip `.draggable` and the box a `.dropDestination`, and highlight the box with `.onDropSessionUpdated` during a drag.

```swift
@State private var basket: [String] = []
@State private var isTargeted = false

HStack {
    ForEach(["Sunflowers", "Tulips", "Ferns"], id: \.self) { plant in
        Text(plant)
            .padding(8)
            .background(.tint.opacity(0.15), in: .capsule)
            .draggable(plant)
    }
}

Text(basket.isEmpty ? "Drop here" : basket.joined(separator: ", "))
    .frame(width: 300, height: 90)
    .background(isTargeted ? Color.accentColor.opacity(0.15) : .clear)
    .dropDestination(for: String.self) { plants, _ in
        basket.append(contentsOf: plants)
    }
    .onDropSessionUpdated { session in
        switch session.phase {
        case .entering, .active: isTargeted = true
        default: isTargeted = false
        }
    }
```

**Note:** Text from other apps works too: select a word in Notes or TextEdit and drag it into the box. Or open a second window above and drag between the two.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Drag your own type, Accept files from the Finder. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/drag-and-drop.md

# Drag and drop

`drag-drop` · macOS · macOS 26.0+
Docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/drag-and-drop.md · HIG: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/drag-and-drop.md

Let people drag content within a window, between windows, and to other apps.

## Use when

- `.draggable` turns a view into something people can drag, and `.dropDestination` makes a view accept drops.
- Both work with `Transferable` types, so the same code handles drags inside a window, between your app's windows, and to and from other apps.
- A type's transfer representations decide what it becomes: your own data when it lands in your app, and plain text or a file in apps that don't know your type.

## Rules

- **Support drag and drop wherever people might try it.** Most people know it and try it everywhere. Text fields and text views already support it.
- **Offer another way to do the same thing.** Some people can't or don't drag. Back every drag with menu commands, like Copy and Paste or Move To.
- **Show whether a destination accepts the drop.** Highlight a destination only while content is over it and only if it can take it. Remove the highlight as soon as the pointer leaves.
- **Move within a container, copy between containers.** Dropping in the same place, like reordering a list, moves the content. Dropping somewhere else copies it, and a drop into another app always copies.
- **Let people drag content to the Finder.** Give it a file format your app can open again, the way Calendar drags an event out as an .ics file.
- **Offer the richest version first.** List your type's representations from highest fidelity to lowest, so each destination takes the best one it understands.

## Pitfalls

- **Common types already work.** `String`, `URL`, and many other system types conform to `Transferable`, so you can drag them without extra code.

## Guide

`.draggable` turns a view into something people can drag, and `.dropDestination` makes a view accept drops. Both work with `Transferable` types, so the same code handles drags inside a window, between your app's windows, and to and from other apps.

### Usage

## Key APIs

`.draggable(_:)`, `.draggable(_:preview:)`, `.dropDestination(for:)`, `.onDropSessionUpdated(_:)`, `Transferable`, `CodableRepresentation`, `ProxyRepresentation`, `.dragConfiguration(_:)`

## Related

`copy-paste`, `file-import-export`, `share-link`, `hover`, `list-styles`

# Copy & paste

Connect the Edit menu's Cut, Copy, Paste, and Delete to your own views.

Also called: clipboard, pasteboard, NSPasteboard, copyable, cuttable, pasteDestination, onCopyCommand, onPasteCommand, onCutCommand, onDeleteCommand.

## Contents

- Use when
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Use when

- Every Mac app has an Edit menu with Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, and Select All, and text fields support them without any code.
- For your own views, `.copyable`, `.cuttable`, and `.pasteDestination` connect those menu items and their shortcuts to your data.
- They use `Transferable`, like drag and drop, so what people copy from your app pastes into other apps, and the other way around.

## Rules

- **Let the Edit menu do the work.** People expect Copy and Paste in the Edit menu and on ⌘C and ⌘V. Extra buttons for the same commands crowd the window.
- **Let people copy text they can't edit.** Content like a caption or an address is often worth pasting somewhere else. Make that text selectable, but not the labels of controls.
- **Call it Delete, not Erase or Clear.** Edit > Delete does what the Delete key does. Unlike Cut, it doesn't put anything on the Clipboard.
- **Support undo.** Menu commands act without asking first. Undo lets people recover from a paste or delete they didn't mean.

## Pitfalls

- **The commands follow focus.** Edit > Copy turns on when the focused view has something to copy, so people click the list first, then press ⌘C.
- **Prefer `Transferable` to item providers.** `.onCopyCommand` and `.onPasteCommand` work with `NSItemProvider`. Apple recommends the `Transferable` modifiers when you can use them.

## Guide

Every Mac app has an Edit menu with Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, and Select All, and text fields support them without any code. For your own views, `.copyable`, `.cuttable`, and `.pasteDestination` connect those menu items and their shortcuts to your data.

They use `Transferable`, like drag and drop, so what people copy from your app pastes into other apps, and the other way around.

### Usage

```swift
@State private var plants = ["Sunflowers", "Tulips", "Ferns"]
@State private var selection = Set<String>()

List(plants, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { plant in
    Text(plant)
}
.copyable(plants.filter { selection.contains($0) })
.pasteDestination(for: String.self) { pasted in
    plants.append(contentsOf: pasted)
}
```

## Key APIs

`.copyable(_:)`, `.cuttable(for:action:)`, `.pasteDestination(for:action:)`, `.onDeleteCommand(perform:)`, `PasteButton(payloadType:)`, `.textSelection(.enabled)`

## Variants

### Cut, copy, and paste list rows

Give a selectable `List` all three modifiers, and let the `.pasteDestination` validator drop unwanted items, like empty lines.

```swift
@State private var plants = ["Sunflowers", "Tulips", "Ferns", "Basil"]
@State private var selection = Set<String>()

List(plants, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { plant in
    Text(plant)
}
.copyable(plants.filter { selection.contains($0) })
.cuttable(for: String.self) {
    let cut = plants.filter { selection.contains($0) }
    plants.removeAll { selection.contains($0) }
    return cut
}
.pasteDestination(for: String.self) { pasted in
    plants.append(contentsOf: pasted)
} validator: { pasted in
    pasted
        .map { $0.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines) }
        .filter { !$0.isEmpty }
}
```

**Note:** Click the list, select a row, and press ⌘C. Paste it into Notes, or copy a word from another app and press ⌘V here.

### The Delete key and Edit > Delete

`.onDeleteCommand` runs when people choose Edit > Delete or press Delete while the view has focus.

```swift
@State private var tags = ["garden", "summer", "seeds", "watering"]
@State private var selection = Set<String>()

List(tags, id: \.self, selection: $selection) { tag in
    Text(tag)
}
.onDeleteCommand {
    tags.removeAll { selection.contains($0) }
}
```

### A Paste button

`PasteButton` reads the Clipboard when clicked and hands you the values of the type you ask for.

```swift
@State private var pasted = ""

PasteButton(payloadType: String.self) { strings in
    pasted = strings.joined(separator: " ")
}
```

**Note:** Add one only where a visible button helps; people look for Edit > Paste and ⌘V first. For a Copy item of your own, like in a context menu, write to `NSPasteboard.general`, since SwiftUI's modifiers only answer the system's Copy command.

### Selectable text

`.textSelection(.enabled)` lets people select a `Text` and copy it with ⌘C or the Edit menu.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Order number")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    Text("W-48213-7")
        .font(.title2.monospaced())
        .textSelection(.enabled)
}
```

## Related

`drag-drop`, `commands`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, `undo-redo`, `text-label`

id: trackpad-gestures
title: Trackpad gestures
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 14.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/magnifygesture.md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pointing-devices.md

# Trackpad gestures

Zoom and rotate with trackpad gestures, plus a way to do both with a mouse.

Also called: pinch, zoom, magnify, rotate, MagnifyGesture, RotateGesture, MagnificationGesture, RotationGesture, NSMagnificationGestureRecognizer, multitouch.

## Contents

- Default code
- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Default code

```swift
@State private var scale = 1.0
@State private var baseScale = 1.0

Image("photo")
    .scaleEffect(scale)
    .gesture(
        MagnifyGesture()
            .onChanged { value in
                scale = baseScale * value.magnification
            }
            .onEnded { _ in
                baseScale = scale
            }
    )
```

**Important:** `value.magnification` starts at 1 for every new pinch. Multiply it by the scale you saved at the end of the last one, or each pinch jumps back to the original size.

## Rules

- **Give mouse users another way.** Pinching and rotating need a trackpad. Add buttons or menu commands that zoom and rotate, so everyone can reach the same result.
- **Don't take over system gestures.** People expect gestures like swiping up for Mission Control to work in every app, and they can customize them in System Settings.
- **Make gestures behave as they do elsewhere.** People expect a gesture to do the same thing in every app, like swiping between pages. A familiar gesture with a new meaning surprises them.

## Pitfalls

- **Scrolling needs no code.** A `ScrollView` scrolls with a trackpad or a mouse; you only add gestures for zooming and rotating.
- **`MagnificationGesture` is deprecated.** So is `RotationGesture`. Use `MagnifyGesture` and `RotateGesture` instead.

## Key APIs

- `MagnifyGesture()`: Pinch with two fingers to zoom.
- `RotateGesture()`: Turn two fingers to rotate.
- `value.magnification`: The scale since the gesture began.
- `value.rotation`: The angle since the gesture began.
- `.simultaneously(with:)`: Zoom and rotate in one motion.
- `.onScrollPhaseChange(_:)`: Tells you when scrolling starts and stops.

## Variants

### Rotate and snap to a right angle

Follow `RotateGesture` while the fingers turn, then snap to the nearest 90° when they lift, like straightening a photo.

```swift
@State private var angle = Angle.zero
@State private var baseAngle = Angle.zero

Image("photo")
    .rotationEffect(angle)
    .gesture(
        RotateGesture()
            .onChanged { angle = baseAngle + $0.rotation }
            .onEnded { _ in
                let quarterTurns = (angle.degrees / 90).rounded()
                withAnimation(.snappy) {
                    angle = .degrees(quarterTurns * 90)
                }
                baseAngle = angle
            }
    )
```

### Know when scrolling stops

`.onScrollPhaseChange` reports when a scroll starts and ends, from a trackpad or a mouse wheel alike.

```swift
@State private var isScrolling = false

ScrollView {
    LazyVStack {
        ForEach(1...40, id: \.self) { Text("Row \($0)") }
    }
}
.onScrollPhaseChange { _, phase in
    isScrolling = phase.isScrolling
}
```

## Related

`hover`, `drag-drop`, `scroll-view`, `animation`

id: file-import-export
title: File import & export
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 11.0+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/fileimporter(ispresented:allowedcontenttypes:oncompletion:).md
hig: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/file-management.md

# File import & export

Show the Mac's open and save panels, and read or write the files people pick.

Also called: open panel, save panel, NSOpenPanel, NSSavePanel, file picker, <input type=file>, download, save as, export, import.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Use the system's open and save panels.** People know how to browse files from the Finder and other apps. Build your own file browser only for a strong reason.
- **Offer Open and New in the File menu.** People expect File > New and File > Open… with ⌘N and ⌘O, even when your window has buttons for them.
- **Name the main button for the task.** If the panel inserts a file rather than opening it, call the button Insert. `.fileDialogConfirmationLabel` sets it.
- **Save work automatically.** Don't make people choose Save to keep their work. Save as they go, and when they close the window or switch apps.

## Pitfalls

- **Canceling calls nothing.** If people cancel, SwiftUI sets the binding back to `false` and skips `onCompletion`. The file exporter calls `onCancellation` instead.
- **This app does it for real.** It has the user-selected read-write entitlement, so the examples below can read and write what you pick.

**Important:** Apple's docs ask you to pair every start call with a stop call. `defer` makes sure the stop call runs, even when reading fails.

## Key APIs

- `.fileImporter(isPresented:…)`: The open panel.
- `.fileExporter(isPresented:item:)`: The save panel, for a `Transferable` item.
- `.fileMover(isPresented:file:)`: A panel that moves a file somewhere else.
- `startAccessingSecurityScopedResource()`: Opens access to a URL from a panel.
- `.fileDialogConfirmationLabel(_:)`: Renames the panel's main button.
- `.fileDialogMessage(_:)`: A message in the panel, like a title.
- `.fileDialogDefaultDirectory(_:)`: The folder the panel opens in.

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
@State private var isImporting = false
@State private var text = ""

Button("Open…") { isImporting = true }
    .fileImporter(isPresented: $isImporting,
                  allowedContentTypes: [.plainText]) { result in
        guard case .success(let url) = result else { return }
        let didAccess = url.startAccessingSecurityScopedResource()
        defer {
            if didAccess { url.stopAccessingSecurityScopedResource() }
        }
        text = (try? String(contentsOf: url, encoding: .utf8)) ?? ""
    }
```

### Pick several files

Pass `allowsMultipleSelection: true` to get an array of URLs, and set a message and button title that fit the task.

```swift
@State private var isImporting = false
@State private var picked: [String] = []

Button("Add Photos…") { isImporting = true }
    .fileImporter(isPresented: $isImporting,
                  allowedContentTypes: [.image],
                  allowsMultipleSelection: true) { result in
        guard case .success(let urls) = result else { return }
        picked = urls.map(\.lastPathComponent)
    }
    .fileDialogMessage("Choose photos for the garden journal.")
    .fileDialogConfirmationLabel("Add")
```

### Save text to a file

`.fileExporter(isPresented:item:)` saves any `Transferable` value, like this `String`.

```swift
@State private var note = "Plant the tulip bulbs before the first frost."
@State private var isExporting = false

Button("Export…") { isExporting = true }
    .fileExporter(isPresented: $isExporting,
                  item: note,
                  contentTypes: [.plainText],
                  defaultFilename: "Garden Note") { result in
        if case .failure(let error) = result {
            print(error.localizedDescription)
        }
    }
```

### Move a file

`.fileMover` asks where to move a file you already have, like a draft from your app's own folder.

```swift
@State private var draft: URL?
@State private var isMoving = false

Button("Move Draft…") { isMoving = true }
    .fileMover(isPresented: $isMoving, file: draft) { result in
        if case .success(let newURL) = result {
            draft = newURL
        }
    }
```

**Note:** The panel only appears when `file` isn't `nil`. Here the sample file starts in this app's temporary folder.

## Related

`app-sandbox`, `drag-drop`, `share-link`, `document-group`, `document-editor`

---
id: state-binding
title: State & Binding
platforms: [macOS]
availability: macOS 10.15+
docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/state.md
---

# State & Binding

@State keeps a value a view owns, and @Binding lets another view change it.

## Contents

- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Pitfalls

- **Declare `@State` as `private`.** Apple's docs say so: setting it from an initializer can conflict with the storage SwiftUI manages for it.
- **With Xcode 27, `@State` is a macro.** It creates its starting value only the first time SwiftUI makes the view, so a model object in `@State` isn't rebuilt each time the parent redraws.
- **Only the owner says `@State`.** Every other view gets either a plain value to read or a `Binding` to write. Two `@State` properties for one value means two copies that drift apart.

## Guide

Every value a view shows has one owner, its **source of truth**. Mark it `@State` in the view that owns it, and SwiftUI stores it and redraws whatever reads it when it changes.

When another view needs to change that value, such as a button in the window's toolbar, pass it a **binding** with `$`. The child declares `@Binding` and reads and writes the owner's value directly, like a controlled input in React.

The window owns `isPlaying`. The play button in its toolbar only has a binding, yet clicking it changes what the window shows.

### Which one to use

- This view creates the value and changes it: `@State private var isPlaying = false`
- A child view changes the owner's value: `@Binding var isPlaying: Bool`, passed as `$isPlaying`
- A child view only shows it: A plain property: `let isPlaying: Bool`
- Several windows or many views share it: An Observable (`observable`) model class, kept in `@State` once

## Key APIs

`@State private var`, `@Binding var`, `$value`, `$draft.title`, `ForEach($items) { $item in }`, `.constant(_:)`

## Variants

### A view option the view owns

Use `@State` for a value only this view needs, like whether a list shows finished tasks. Controls take `$showsCompleted`.

```swift
@State private var showsCompleted = true

let tasks = ["Write outline", "Record intro", "Edit episode"]
let finished: Set = ["Write outline"]

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Toggle("Show completed", isOn: $showsCompleted)
    ForEach(tasks, id: \.self) { task in
        if showsCompleted || !finished.contains(task) {
            Label(task, systemImage: finished.contains(task) ? "checkmark.circle.fill" : "circle")
        }
    }
}
```

### Selection is a binding too

`List(selection:)` writes the selected rows into your `@State`. With a `Set`, people can select several rows on the Mac without an edit mode.

```swift
struct Mailbox: Identifiable {
    let id: String
    let name: String
    let symbol: String
}

let mailboxes = [
    Mailbox(id: "inbox", name: "Inbox", symbol: "tray"),
    Mailbox(id: "flagged", name: "Flagged", symbol: "flag"),
    Mailbox(id: "drafts", name: "Drafts", symbol: "doc"),
    Mailbox(id: "sent", name: "Sent", symbol: "paperplane"),
]

@State private var selection: Set<Mailbox.ID> = ["inbox"]

List(mailboxes, selection: $selection) { mailbox in
    Label(mailbox.name, systemImage: mailbox.symbol)
}
Text("\(selection.count) selected")
```

**Note:** Bind to a single optional ID instead of a `Set` when only one row can be selected at a time.

### Bind to one property of a struct

Keep related fields in one struct in `@State`. `$draft.title` is a binding to just that field, so each control edits its own part.

```swift
struct NoteDraft {
    var title = "Weekly review"
    var isPinned = false
    var color = Color.yellow
}

@State private var draft = NoteDraft()

Form {
    TextField("Title", text: $draft.title)
    Toggle("Pin to top", isOn: $draft.isPinned)
    ColorPicker("Color", selection: $draft.color)
}
```

### A binding for each row

`ForEach($tasks) { $task in … }` hands every row a binding to its own element, so a checkbox can tick off one task in the array.

```swift
struct TaskItem: Identifiable {
    let id = UUID()
    var title: String
    var isDone = false
}

@State private var tasks = [
    TaskItem(title: "Export the audio"),
    TaskItem(title: "Write show notes", isDone: true),
    TaskItem(title: "Upload the episode"),
]

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    ForEach($tasks) { $task in
        Toggle(task.title, isOn: $task.isDone)
    }
```

# State & Binding

`state-binding` · macOS · macOS 10.15+
Docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/state.md

@State keeps a value a view owns, and @Binding lets another view change it.

## Pitfalls

- **Declare `@State` as `private`.** Apple's docs say so: setting it from an initializer can conflict with the storage SwiftUI manages for it.
- **With Xcode 27, `@State` is a macro.** It creates its starting value only the first time SwiftUI makes the view, so a model object in `@State` isn't rebuilt each time the parent redraws.
- **Only the owner says `@State`.** Every other view gets either a plain value to read or a `Binding` to write. Two `@State` properties for one value means two copies that drift apart.

## Guide

Every value a view shows has one owner, its **source of truth**. Mark it `@State` in the view that owns it, and SwiftUI stores it and redraws whatever reads it when it changes.

When another view needs to change that value, such as a button in the window's toolbar, pass it a **binding** with `$`. The child declares `@Binding` and reads and writes the owner's value directly, like a controlled input in React.

The window owns `isPlaying`. The play button in its toolbar only has a binding, yet clicking it changes what the window shows.

### Which one to use

- This view creates the value and changes it: `@State private var isPlaying = false`
- A child view changes the owner's value: `@Binding var isPlaying: Bool`, passed as `$isPlaying`
- A child view only shows it: A plain property: `let isPlaying: Bool`
- Several windows or many views share it: An Observable (`observable`) model class, kept in `@State` once

## Key APIs

`@State private var`, `@Binding var`, `$value`, `$draft.title`, `ForEach($items) { $item in }`, `.constant(_:)`

# Animation

`animation` · macOS · macOS 14.0+
Docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/animations.md · HIG: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion.md

Springs and transitions that stay quick and quiet under a pointer and in big windows.

## Default code

```swift
@State private var showsDetails = false

VStack {
    Button(showsDetails ? "Hide Details" : "Show Details") {
        withAnimation(.snappy) {
            showsDetails.toggle()
        }
    }
    if showsDetails {
        Text("Recorded on October 12")
            .transition(.opacity)
    }
}
```

**Note:** Change state inside `withAnimation`, not the view. SwiftUI works out what moved and animates it, like a CSS transition on whatever the change affects.

## Rules

- **Add motion for a reason.** Use it to show where something came from or that something changed. Motion just for show distracts people and can make some of them feel unwell.
- **Skip motion on things people do all the time.** Standard controls already animate on their own. A pointer passes over custom rows constantly, so keep their hover feedback brief or leave the motion out.
- **Never make people wait for an animation.** Let them click again, or move on, while it plays. Springs handle an interruption smoothly, so don't block input until one finishes.
- **Make motion optional.** With Reduce Motion on, swap slides and zooms for fades and calm the bounce. Don't let motion be the only way people learn something happened.

## Pitfalls

- **Springs keep their speed when interrupted.** Click again mid-move and the next spring starts from where the view is, moving as fast as it was.
- **`withAnimation` animates what the change touches.** Every view that redraws because of the state you change inside it animates, wherever it is in the window.

## Key APIs

`withAnimation(.snappy) { }`, `.animation(_:value:)`, `.spring(duration:bounce:)`, `.smooth`, `.snappy`, `.bouncy`, `.transition(_:)`, `.onHover { }`, `.contentTransition(_:)`, `\.accessibilityReduceMotion`

# Charts & Maps

Swift Charts with a selectable plot, and a MapKit map that fills a window.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Say what the chart shows in words.** A short headline above the chart gives the main message at a glance, so people don't have to read the plot to get it.
- **Don't hide important values behind interaction.** Selecting a point to see its value is a nice extra. Anything people must know, like a total or a trend, belongs on the chart itself.
- **Keep charts simple.** Too much data in one chart buries what matters. Let people choose a range or a series when they want more detail.
- **Let people move around the map.** People expect to zoom and pan any map. Don't cover it with views that block those gestures, and keep the Apple logo and legal link visible.
- **Mute the map when your content is the point.** The muted emphasis style lowers the map's colors so your markers and overlays stand out.

## Pitfalls

- **Charts are accessible by default.** Swift Charts gives VoiceOver the marks and an Audio Graph; add a title and a short summary that say what the chart is for.
- **Maps load over the network.** A sandboxed app needs the Outgoing Connections (Client) entitlement. See App Sandbox (`app-sandbox`).

## Key APIs

`Chart(data) { }`, `LineMark`, `BarMark`, `PointMark`, `.chartXSelection(value:)`, `RuleMark(x:)`, `Map(initialPosition:) { }`, `Marker(_:systemImage:coordinate:)`, `.mapControls { }`, `.mapStyle(_:)`

## Variants

### Usage

```swift
import Charts

struct DayCount: Identifiable {
    let day: Date
    let downloads: Int
    var id: Date { day }
}

struct DownloadsChart: View {
    let days: [DayCount]

    var body: some View {
        Chart(days) { day in
            LineMark(
                x: .value("Day", day.day, unit: .day),
                y: .value("Downloads", day.downloads)
            )
        }
    }
}
```

### Select a day to see its value

Bind `.chartXSelection(value:)` to a `Date?`, then draw a `RuleMark` with an annotation at the selected day.

```swift
import Charts

@State private var selectedDay: Date?

Chart(days) { day in
    LineMark(
        x: .value("Day", day.day, unit: .day),
        y: .value("Downloads", day.downloads)
    )
    if let selectedDay {
        RuleMark(x: .value("Day", selectedDay, unit: .day))
            .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
            .annotation(position: .top, overflowResolution: .init(x: .fit(to: .chart), y: .disabled)) {
                Text(selectedDay, format: .dateTime.month().day())
                    .font(.caption)
            }
    }
}
.chartXSelection(value: $selectedDay)
.frame(height: 200)
```

**Note:** The selection is a raw x value, not one of your data points. Look up the nearest day yourself to show its count.

### Compare categories with bars

Use `BarMark` to compare totals, and state the takeaway above the chart, the way the guidelines suggest.

```swift
import Charts

struct PlatformShare: Identifiable {
    let name: String
    let downloads: Int
    var id: String { name }
}

let shares = [
    PlatformShare(name: "Mac", downloads: 1840),
    PlatformShare(name: "iPhone", downloads: 1260),
    PlatformShare(name: "iPad", downloads: 610),
]

VStack(alignment: .leading) {
    Text("Most downloads come from the Mac")
        .font(.headline)
    Chart(shares) { share in
        BarMark(
            x: .value("Downloads", share.downloads),
            y: .value("Platform", share.name)
        )
        .foregroundStyle(by: .value("Platform", share.name))
    }
    .chartLegend(.hidden)
    .frame(height: 140)
}
```

### A map with your places

Give `Map` a starting region and list a `Marker` for each place. People can pan, zoom, and rotate it as in Maps.

```swift
import MapKit

struct Cafe: Identifiable {
    let name: String
    let coordinate: CLLocationCoordinate2D
    var id: String { name }
}

let cafes = [
    Cafe(name: "Ferry Building", coordinate: .init(latitude: 37.7955, longitude: -122.3937)),
    Cafe(name: "Union Square", coordinate: .init(latitude: 37.7880, longitude: -122.4075)),
]

let region = MKCoordinateRegion(
    center: .init(latitude: 37.79, longitude: -122.40),
    span: .init(latitudeDelta: 0.04, longitudeDelta: 0.04)
)

Map(initialPosition: .region(region)) {
    ForEach(cafes) { cafe in
        Marker(cafe.name, systemImage: "cup.and.saucer.fill", coordinate: cafe.coordinate)
            .tint(.brown)
    }
}
.mapStyle(.standard(emphasis: .muted))
.mapControls {
    MapZoomStepper()
    MapCompass()
    MapScaleView()
}
.frame(height: 260)
```

# Library window

A sidebar, a sortable table, and an inspector: the classic window for browsing a library.

## Built from

NavigationSplitView
├── sidebar: List(selection:)
│   ├── Section("Library")
│   └── Section("Playlists")
└── detail: Table(selection:sortOrder:)
    ├── .searchable(text:)
    ├── .toolbar { … }
    └── .inspector(isPresented:)
        └── Form

## Rules

- **Use familiar symbols in the sidebar.** A symbol next to each item helps people scan the list and find a place again. Leave their color to the accent color people chose.
- **Keep the sidebar to two levels.** Use short section headers for the groups. If your data goes deeper, add a content column between the sidebar and the details.
- **Let people hide the side panes, but show them at first.** Some people want room for the content, so offer a toolbar button and a View menu command. Start with the sidebar visible so people find it.
- **Don't put key actions at the bottom of the sidebar.** People often move windows so the bottom edge is off screen.

## Pitfalls

- **The table doesn't sort for you.** It shows the sort in its headers and updates `sortOrder`, and you sort your array when that changes.
- **The inspector remembers itself.** A trailing-column inspector has its shown or hidden state restored for you.
- **Add the standard commands.** `SidebarCommands()` adds the built-in sidebar commands, and `InspectorCommands()` adds one that shows and hides the inspector with ⌃⌘I.

## Key APIs

# Settings window

A Settings window with a toolbar of panes, ready to copy into your app.

## Built from

Settings
└── SettingsView
    └── TabView(selection:)
        ├── Tab("General")
        │   └── Form
        ├── Tab("Accounts")
        │   └── List + add and remove
        └── Tab("Advanced")
            └── Form

## Rules

- **Don't copy system settings.** Scrolling, accessibility, and sign-in methods belong to System Settings. A copy in your app suggests the system choice doesn't apply.
- **Offer as few settings as you can.** Good defaults mean most people never open the window. Every extra option makes the one people want harder to find.
- **Keep the toolbar of panes still.** Don't let people customize it or hide it, and always show which pane is active. People find settings by where they are.
- **Reopen the last pane.** People often come back to adjust a related setting. Bind the `TabView` to `@AppStorage`, as the block does.
- **Leave task options in the window.** Sorting, filters, and showing a sidebar belong next to the content they change, not in Settings.

## Pitfalls

- **`@AppStorage` keeps every window in sync.** A setting changed here shows up in your other windows right away, and it's saved for the next launch.
- **The `TabView` becomes the toolbar.** Inside `Settings`, its tabs turn into the toolbar of panes, so you don't build that toolbar yourself.

## Key APIs

`Settings { }`, `TabView(selection:)`, `Tab(_:systemImage:value:)`, `@AppStorage`, `.formStyle(.grouped)`, `SettingsLink`

# Menu bar utility

`menu-bar-utility` · macOS · macOS 14.0+
Docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/menubarextra.md · HIG: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/the-menu-bar.md

A small app that lives in the menu bar and opens a panel when clicked.

## Rules

- **Use a symbol for the menu bar icon.** A template symbol is drawn in the menu bar's own colors, so it looks right in light and dark menu bars and when it's highlighted.
- **Show a menu unless you need more.** Clicking an extra usually opens a menu. Use the window style only when the feature is too rich for menu items, like this timer.
- **Let people choose to show it.** Put a “Show in menu bar” setting in Settings, and offer it during setup so people find it.
- **Don't count on it being visible.** The system hides extras when the menu bar runs out of room. Make the same features reachable from your app's windows or its Dock menu too.

## Pitfalls

- **No Dock icon.** For an app that lives only in the menu bar, set `LSUIElement` to `YES` in its Info.plist, so it stays out of the Dock and the app switcher.
- **Removing the extra quits the app.** When an app's only scene is a `MenuBarExtra` and people remove it from the menu bar, the system ends the app.

# Document editor

`document-editor` · macOS · macOS 12.0+
Docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/documentgroup.md · HIG: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/file-management.md

A text editor that opens, saves, and creates files, with a toolbar for formatting.

## Rules

- **Save for people.** Don't make people press Save to keep their work. Save as they go, and keep the toolbar for the tools they use while writing.
- **Create and open from the File menu.** People expect New and Open in the File menu with their usual shortcuts. A document app gets them without extra code.
- **Call a new document “Untitled”.** Let people name it when they save it, in the save panel, along with where it goes.
- **Use the standard open and save panels.** People know the Finder's way of browsing files. Build your own file browser only for a strong reason.

## Pitfalls

- **Every document app declares its types.** Add Document Types (`CFBundleDocumentTypes`) to the Info pane, so the Finder knows which files your app opens.
- **Use the binding, not the file.** `configuration.fileURL` is fine for showing a name, but read and write only through your `FileDocument`, or you'll fight SwiftUI for the file.

# Welcome window

The window a document app shows at launch, with New, Open, and recent files.

## Built from

Window("Welcome to Notes", id:)
├── .windowStyle(.hiddenTitleBar)

    ├── icon, name, version

## Rules

- **Put people back where they were.** If documents were open when people quit, reopen them instead of greeting them again. With `.presented`, the welcome window shows only when nothing comes back.
- **Offer recent files next to Open.** Most of the time people want what they had yesterday. A list of recent documents saves a trip through the open panel.
- **Get out of the way fast.** People want to start right away. Keep the window to a few ways in, so they can pick one and get to work.

## Pitfalls

- **It appears only when nothing is restored.** With `.defaultLaunchBehavior(.presented)`, the welcome window shows at launch when no document windows come back, and when people click the Dock icon with no windows open.
- **Recent files come from AppKit.** SwiftUI has no list of recent documents, so the block reads AppKit's `NSDocumentController.shared.recentDocumentURLs`.

## Pitfalls

- **It appears only when nothing is restored.** With `.defaultLaunchBehavior(.presented)`, the welcome window shows at launch when no document windows come back, and when people click the Dock icon with no windows open.

# Empty states

`empty-states` · macOS · macOS 14.0+
Docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/contentunavailableview.md · HIG: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/writing.md

What a sidebar, table, or search shows when there's nothing to show yet.

## Rules

- **Say what to do next, and give a button for it.** An empty window is daunting when the next step isn't clear. Name the action and put it right there.
- **Show progress while loading, not an empty state.** “No Items” while data is still on its way looks like a problem. Show a progress indicator until you know the list is empty.
- **Keep important information out of it.** An empty state goes away as soon as there's content, and anything in it goes too.

## Pitfalls

- **Overlay it, don't replace the list.** Put `ContentUnavailableView` in an `.overlay` on the empty `List` or `Table`, so the column headers, toolbar, and search field stay put.
- **`.search` fills in the words for you.** `ContentUnavailableView.search(text:)` builds a no-results message that quotes what people typed.

## Key APIs

- `ContentUnavailableView(_:systemImage:)`: A title and symbol, for simple cases.
- `ContentUnavailableView { } description: { }`: Adds a line about what to do.
- `actions: { Button… }`: Buttons under the message.
- `.search(text:)`: The standard no-results message.
- `.overlay { }`: Shows it on top of the empty list or table.

# Windows & Layout

Lay out windows that people move, resize, and stack beside other apps.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Keep important controls away from the bottom edge.** People often drag a window partly below the screen, which hides whatever sits at its bottom. Put actions in the toolbar or near the top.
- **Put what matters most at the top leading corner.** People read a window from the top and from the leading side, so the first thing they should see goes there.
- **Use a bottom bar only for a little status.** A bottom bar suits a short summary of the window, like a count of items. If you have more to show, use an inspector instead.
- **Let the system draw the window.** People know the standard frame, buttons, and title bar. A custom copy that doesn't match exactly makes the whole app feel broken.
- **Open new windows when they help, not by default.** A second window is great for comparing or keeping context, like a draft beside the message it answers. Offer Open in New Window in the File menu or a context menu instead of opening one every time.
- **Call it a window.** In anything people read, say window, whatever kind it is. Words like scene describe your code, not what people see.

## Pitfalls

- **Try the smallest and largest sizes first.** Apple suggests testing the extremes before the sizes in between, since that's where clipping shows up.
- **People decide where windows go.** People typically run several apps at once, so don't count on your window filling the screen or staying where it opened.

## Guide

On the Mac, people keep several apps open at once. They move, resize, minimize, and stack windows to suit their work, so your layout has to hold up at any size you allow, next to windows from other apps.

### Parts of a window

- Frame: The top of the window, with the close, minimize, and zoom buttons and often a toolbar. People drag it to move the window.
- Body: Your content. People can usually resize the window by dragging its edges.
- Bottom bar: Rare. A thin strip under the content for a little status, like Finder's count of items and free space.

### Window states

Only one window takes your typing at a time. The Mac draws the three states differently, so people can tell which window is in front and which one gets their input.

- Key: The window that receives keyboard input. Its close, minimize, and zoom buttons are in color. Only one window on screen is key.
- Main: The app's frontmost window. It's usually also key, unless a panel such as Fonts is taking input.
- Inactive: Any window in the background. Its window buttons turn gray and it drops its materials, so it looks farther away.

**Note:** System controls switch appearance on their own. Custom views can read `appearsActive`, as in the last example below.

## Key APIs

`.defaultSize(width:height:)`, `.windowResizability(_:)`, `.frame(minWidth:minHeight:)`, `.scenePadding()`, `ViewThatFits`, `\.appearsActive`, `.backgroundExtensionEffect()`

## Variants

### Choose a starting size and a minimum

Use `.defaultSize(width:height:)` on the scene for the first launch, and a minimum `.frame` on the content so the layout never breaks.

```swift
@main
struct TripsApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
                .frame(minWidth: 480, minHeight: 320)
        }
        .defaultSize(width: 900, height: 600)
    }
}
```

### Size the window to its content

Use `.windowResizability(.contentSize)` for a window that should stay the size of what's inside, like a small utility window.

```swift
Window("Converter", id: "converter") {
    ConverterView()
        .frame(width: 320, height: 160)
}
.windowResizability(.contentSize)
```

### Use the Mac's margins

Apply `.scenePadding()` to a window's root view for the recommended space around its content, instead of picking a number.

```swift
VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
    Text("Lisbon")
        .font(.title2)
    Text("4 nights · 2 travelers")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
}
.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
.scenePadding()
```

### Rearrange when the window narrows

`ViewThatFits` tries each layout in order and keeps the first one that fits, so a narrow window stacks what a wide one shows side by side.

```swift
ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal) {
    HStack(alignment: .top, spacing: 20) {
        TripSummary()
        TripStops()
    }
    VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 16) {
        TripSummary()
        TripStops()
    }
}
```

**Note:** Keep the same features at every size. Only how many show at once should change, not what the window can do.

More variants, left out to keep this file short: Tone down custom accents in inactive windows. Apple's docs: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/windows.md

# Color & Accent

Semantic colors that adapt, and an accent color people choose for every app.

Also called: accent color, tint, AccentColor, brand color, theme, system colors, semantic colors, NSColor, labelColor, controlAccentColor.

## Contents

- Rules
- Pitfalls
- Guide
- Key APIs
- Variants
- Related

## Rules

- **Use semantic colors for what they're named for.** Each one is defined by its job, so it adapts correctly. Don't borrow the separator color for text, or a label color for a background.
- **Don't rely on color alone.** Pair color with a symbol or a word, so people who can't tell the colors apart still get the message.
- **Let the person's accent color lead.** People can pick an accent color that applies to every app. Use `Color.accentColor` and the default control styles, so buttons and selection follow their choice.
- **Give each color one meaning.** If your brand color marks things people can click, don't also use it for plain text. Mixed meanings make people guess.
- **Use color sparingly on Liquid Glass.** Symbols and text in a toolbar are monochrome by default. To call out the main action, color its background, as a prominent button does, rather than its symbol or text.
- **Use the system color picker.** If people choose colors in your app, `ColorPicker` opens the standard Colors panel, where their saved colors are waiting.

## Pitfalls

- **Never hard-code a system color's value.** Apple adjusts them between releases and for each appearance. Use `Color.red`, not the RGB numbers it has today.
- **Your accent shows only with Multicolor.** Check your app with a few other accent colors chosen in System Settings, since anyone who picks one sees your app that way.

## Guide

Mac colors are named for what they do, not how they look: label, separator, window background, selected content. Each one has values for light, dark, and Increase Contrast, so a window built from them adapts on its own. On top of that, people choose an **accent color** in System Settings, and it shows up in every app's buttons, selection, and sidebar icons.

### Your accent color or theirs

- Multicolor: When people leave the accent color on Multicolor, the system uses your app's accent color, from the `AccentColor` set in your asset catalog.
- Any other choice: Their color replaces yours everywhere: buttons, selection, and sidebar icons. A sidebar icon you gave a fixed color keeps it.
- .tint(_:): Always respected. Use it when a color carries meaning, like red for a destructive action, not to force your brand.

### Semantic colors

Live, in light and dark. The first ones are SwiftUI styles; the rest come from AppKit's `NSColor`.

### System colors

Each has its own light and dark value, tuned for contrast. Use them by name.

## Key APIs

- `Color.accentColor`: The person's accent color, or yours with Multicolor.
- `.tint(_:)`: A color with meaning that's always respected.
- `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`: Label colors that adapt: `.primary` to `.quaternary`.
- `.separator`, `.link`, `.selection`: Semantic styles for lines, links, and selection.
- `Color(nsColor:)`: AppKit's semantic colors, like `.textBackgroundColor`.
- `.listItemTint(_:)`: A fixed color for one sidebar icon.
- `ColorPicker`: The system's color well and Colors panel.

## Variants

### Use the accent color

A `.borderedProminent` button fills with `Color.accentColor`: yours with Multicolor, the person's choice otherwise.

```swift
HStack {
    Button("Cancel") { }
    Button("Book Trip") { }
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
}
```

**Note:** Set your accent in the asset catalog's `AccentColor` color set. Xcode's templates name it for you.

### Give a control a fixed meaning

`.tint(.red)` keeps a destructive button red whatever accent color people pick.

```swift
HStack {
    Button("Keep Trip") { }
    Button("Delete Trip", role: .destructive) { }
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
        .tint(.red)
}
```

**Note:** On the Mac, `.borderedProminent` tints the button's background, and `.bordered` doesn't tint at all.

### Keep one sidebar icon's color

Sidebar icons follow the accent color, so save `.listItemTint(_:)` for the rare icon whose color means something.

```swift
List {
    Label("Inbox", systemImage: "tray")
    Label("Important", systemImage: "star")
        .listItemTint(.yellow)
    Label("Sent", systemImage: "paperplane")
}
.listStyle(.sidebar)
```

### Use AppKit's semantic colors

`Color(nsColor:)` brings in Mac colors SwiftUI doesn't name, like `.textBackgroundColor` behind editable text.

```swift
Text("Bring a light jacket for the evenings.")
    .padding(10)
    .frame(width: 260, height: 70, alignment: .topLeading)
    .background(Color(nsColor: .textBackgroundColor))
    .border(.separator)
```
